articles.title: Current accounts explained
articles.summary: Sort codes, account numbers, debit cards, Confirmation of Payee and how to pick an everyday account.

body.text: Your current account is where your pay lands and your bills leave from. Pick one that's free, has a good app and doesn't punish you for the occasional slip.
The numbers that matter

items: Sort code (6 digits): identifies your bank and branch.
Account number (8 digits): identifies your account.
Debit card: spends your own money. It's not credit, so it doesn't build a credit history the same way.

body.text: Confirmation of Payee

When you pay someone new, your bank checks that the name you typed matches the account. If it says “no match” or “close match”, stop and check with the person on a number you already have. It's one of the best scam blockers there is.
What to look for in an everyday account

items: No monthly fee (or one you get value from).
A clear app with spending pots, notifications and card freeze.
Fair overdraft pricing, if you ever need one.
Fee-free spending abroad if you travel.
FSCS protection: check the bank is UK-authorised.

body.text: Many hunters keep two accounts: a main one for bills and pay, and a spare one used only for switching. Your real finances never get disrupted.
Why banks check your ID
Anti-money-laundering rules require banks to verify who you are. Have your passport or driving licence ready. Some applications also run a credit check (see “Your credit score”).

articles.title: How a CASS switch works
articles.summary: The 7-working-day switch, choosing a date, the Switch Guarantee and payment redirection.

body.text: The Current Account Switch Service (CASS) moves your whole current account to a new bank for you: salary, Direct Debits and standing orders. It's free, and it's run by Pay.UK, the industry body behind UK payments.

items: Takes 7 working days, on a date you choose
Free for customers
Your old account is closed and payments sent to it are redirected
Covered by the Current Account Switch Guarantee

body.text: How a full switch works

items: Open the new account and choose the option to switch from another bank.
Enter your old account details and pick a switch date (at least 7 working days away).
CASS moves your Direct Debits and standing orders. Incoming payments such as your salary are redirected automatically, but it's still worth giving your employer your new details.
On the switch date your old account closes and any balance moves across.
Payments still sent to your old details are redirected to the new account.

body.text: The Switch Guarantee
If anything goes wrong with the switch, you're refunded any interest and charges it causes on either account. That's why a full CASS switch is much safer than moving things by hand.
Full vs partial switch
A partial switch copies some payments across but keeps your old account open. It isn't a CASS full switch, so it doesn't close the old account and usually won't qualify for switch bonuses.
Working days don't include weekends or bank holidays. If an offer has a deadline, count carefully, especially around Christmas and Easter.
Choose a switch date that isn't right before a big bill or payday, so you can check everything has moved before money starts flowing.

articles.title: Bank switch bonuses: the rules
articles.summary: Pay-in amounts, active Direct Debits, eligibility windows, clawbacks and how to never miss a bonus.

body.text: Banks sometimes pay you a cash bonus to switch your current account to them. It's legitimate: they're competing for customers. But every offer has rules, and missing one means no bonus.
The usual conditions

items: A full switch using CASS, often within a deadline (e.g. 30 or 60 days).
Pay in a minimum amount, often from an external account, within a time limit.
Have a set number of active Direct Debits. “Active” usually means at least one payment has actually gone out.
Not have held an account with that bank (or bank group), or claimed a bonus from them, within a set period.
Sometimes: log into the app, use the debit card, or keep the account open for a period.

body.text: The 5-minute checklist before you apply

items: Read the full terms on the bank's own site, not a summary.
Check eligibility: the exclusion window, and whether sister brands count as the same bank.
Write down every condition and its deadline.
Set Direct Debits up early, so they've collected before the deadline.
Set a calendar reminder a week before each deadline.

body.text: Clawbacks
Some offers can take the bonus back if you close the account within a set time. Look for words like “reclaim” or “withdraw the payment” in the small print.
Credit files

Many current account applications involve a hard credit search, especially with an overdraft. A few spaced-out switches are fine for most people, but avoid stacking applications before a mortgage or big loan.
Offers change fast. Money Hunters shows live offers with the date each was last checked. Always confirm on the provider's own page before applying.
Try the switch simulator in Coinsworth Bank in the game first: it walks you through every rule with a made-up offer.

articles.title: Direct Debits & standing orders
articles.summary: What they are, the Direct Debit Guarantee, and cheap ways to meet switch requirements.

body.text: A Direct Debit lets a company collect money from your account on agreed dates. The amount can change, but they must tell you in advance.
Direct Debit vs standing order

items: Direct Debit: the company pulls the money. It can vary. Covered by the Direct Debit Guarantee.
Standing order: you push a fixed amount on set dates. You control it.
Card payment: neither of the above, so it doesn't count towards switch bonus rules.

body.text: The Direct Debit Guarantee
If an error is made in the amount or date of a Direct Debit, your bank must refund you straight away. You can cancel a Direct Debit at any time through your bank.
Meeting switch bonus rules

Most switch offers need a number of active Direct Debits. Usually that means each one has collected at least one payment. Everyday bills (phone, energy, council tax, gym) count. Set them up on the new account early.
Before switching, check your bank app for Direct Debits you don't recognise or don't need. A switch is a good moment for a clear-out.

articles.title: Overdrafts: the real cost
articles.summary: Arranged vs unarranged, interest rates, and how to get out of your overdraft.

body.text: An overdraft lets you spend more than you have. Since April 2020, FCA rules mean overdrafts are priced with a single annual interest rate. Banks can't charge fixed daily or monthly overdraft fees, and unarranged overdrafts can't cost more than arranged ones.

items: Around 40% a year is common for arranged overdrafts
£500 overdrawn all year at about 40% costs roughly £200
Banks must show an APR so you can compare

body.text: Why overdrafts are expensive borrowing
An overdraft feels like part of your balance, but at typical rates it costs far more than most personal loans or a 0% card cleared in time.
Getting out of your overdraft

items: Find your real balance: your balance minus the overdraft.
Turn off or lower the limit gradually so you can't slide back.
Cut one or two non-essentials and put that money towards the overdraft each payday.
If it's large, compare a cheaper way to borrow, but only if you won't run the overdraft up again.
If you're struggling, talk to your bank. It must help customers in financial difficulty.

body.text: If borrowing feels out of control, get free help from StepChange, Citizens Advice or MoneyHelper. Never pay a company for debt advice.

articles.title: Interest rates explained
articles.summary: AER, gross, monthly vs annual interest, and inflation's effect on your savings.

body.text: Interest rates look simple, but the way they're quoted changes what you actually earn. Here's how to compare like for like.
The terms

items: AER (Annual Equivalent Rate): what you'd earn over a year including interest on interest. Use this to compare accounts.
Gross: the rate before tax.
Fixed vs variable: a fixed rate is locked for a term, and a variable rate can change at any time.
Easy access, notice and fixed term: how quickly you can get your money out.
£10,000 at 4% AER earns about £400 in a year
The same £10,000 at 1% earns about £100
Moving savings can be the easiest money you'll ever make

body.text: Watch the small print

items: Teaser or bonus rates that drop after a few months.
Tiered rates where the headline rate only applies to the first slice of your money.
Withdrawal limits on “easy access” accounts.
Interest paid monthly vs yearly. Monthly grows very slightly faster if you leave it in.

body.text: Inflation

If prices rise faster than your interest rate, your savings lose buying power even as the balance grows. That's why the rate matters so much, and why long-term money may belong in investments rather than cash.
Set a reminder for the day any bonus rate ends, then move your money if the rate drops.

articles.title: Regular savers
articles.summary: High-rate monthly saving accounts and why the headline rate overstates what you earn.

body.text: Regular savers pay a high rate on money you add each month, up to a cap. They're a great habit-builder, but the headline rate is misleading.
Why you earn less than you'd think

You only pay in a little at a time, so most of your money isn't there for the whole year. At 6% AER, paying in £200 a month for 12 months (£2,400 in total) earns roughly £78, not £144, because your average balance is only about £1,300.
Typical rules

items: A monthly maximum (and sometimes a minimum).
Missed months can't be made up later.
Withdrawals may be limited or close the account.
Often you need a current account with the same bank.
A fixed term (usually 12 months), then the money moves to a lower rate.

body.text: Use a regular saver to drip money in from your main account, while keeping the rest of your savings in the best easy-access account.

articles.title: ISAs
articles.summary: Cash and Stocks & Shares ISAs, the annual allowance and flexible ISAs.

body.text: An ISA (Individual Savings Account) is a tax-free wrapper. Interest, dividends and gains inside it are free of UK tax, and you don't need to declare them.

items: Overall ISA allowance: £20,000 per tax year (6 April to 5 April)
From 6 April 2027, under-65s can put a maximum of £12,000 a year into Cash ISAs (the overall £20,000 stays)
Unused allowance can't be carried forward

body.text: The main types

items: Cash ISA: savings, with interest tax-free.
Stocks & Shares ISA: investments, with gains and dividends tax-free. Value can go up or down.
Lifetime ISA: for a first home or retirement, with a government bonus. It has strict rules and penalties, so read the details first.
Innovative Finance ISA: higher-risk lending products.

body.text: Rules that catch people out

items: The £20,000 limit is for all your ISAs combined.
Moving an ISA? Use an ISA transfer. Withdrawing it yourself can lose the tax-free status.
With a non-flexible ISA, money you withdraw and put back counts again towards your allowance. Flexible ISAs let you replace it in the same tax year.

body.text: Do you even need one?

Most people get a Personal Savings Allowance (£1,000 of interest tax-free for basic-rate taxpayers, £500 for higher-rate). If your interest is below that, a normal savings account paying more may beat a Cash ISA. For investments, a Stocks & Shares ISA is almost always worth it.
ISA rules change. Figures were checked in October 2026. Check gov.uk before each new tax year.

articles.title: Premium Bonds
articles.summary: How the prize draw works, what's guaranteed and who they suit.

body.text: Premium Bonds are run by NS&I and backed by HM Treasury. Instead of interest, each £1 bond gets entered into a monthly prize draw.

items: Hold from £25 up to £50,000
Prizes are tax-free
100% backed by HM Treasury
You can cash them in at any time

body.text: The trade-off

The advertised “prize fund rate” is an average. Most holders with small amounts win little or nothing in many months, so your actual return can be well below a good savings account. Big wins are very rare.
Who they suit

items: Higher-rate taxpayers who've used their Personal Savings Allowance (prizes are tax-free).
People with savings above the FSCS limit who want Treasury backing.
People who enjoy the draw and accept a lower expected return.

body.text: Compare the prize fund rate with the best easy-access rate after tax. For many people, a savings account wins.

articles.title: Building an emergency fund
articles.summary: How much to keep, where to keep it and how to build it fast.

body.text: An emergency fund is cash set aside for the unexpected: a broken boiler, a car repair, a gap between jobs. It stops a bad week becoming expensive debt.
How much?
A common guide is 3–6 months of essential spending (rent, bills, food, transport). Start smaller: even £500 to £1,000 covers many surprises.
Where to keep it

items: Easy access, so you can get it within a day.
A separate account or pot, so you don't dip into it.
Cash, not investments, because shares might be down exactly when you need the money.
An FSCS-protected bank or building society.

body.text: How to build it

items: Set a starter goal (e.g. £500).
Automate a transfer the day you're paid.
Add windfalls: tax refunds, switch bonuses, cashback payouts.
Refill it after you use it.

body.text: Bank switch bonuses are a great way to kick-start an emergency fund.

articles.title: Is my money safe? The FSCS
articles.summary: What's protected, the limit, and banking licences.

body.text: The Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS) protects your money if a UK-authorised bank, building society or credit union fails.

items: Up to £120,000 per person, per banking licence (since 1 December 2025)
Joint accounts: up to £120,000 for each person
Higher temporary protection for some life events (like a house sale) for a limited time

body.text: Banking licences
Some bank brands share one licence, so savings across them share one £120,000 limit. If you hold a lot, check which brands belong together.
What's not covered

items: Crypto, and money held on crypto exchanges.
Most investment losses from normal market falls (FSCS protects against firm failure, not bad performance).
Firms that aren't UK-authorised.

body.text: Use the FSCS online protection checker to see whether a provider is covered.

articles.title: Investing basics
articles.summary: Risk and return, shares, funds, diversification and time in the market.

body.text: Investing means putting money into things like shares, bonds or funds, in the hope it grows faster than cash over the long term. It comes with risk: values go down as well as up, and you could get back less than you put in.
The building blocks

items: Shares: part-ownership of a company. Higher potential returns, bigger swings.
Bonds: loans to governments or companies that pay interest. Usually steadier.
Funds: one product holding many shares or bonds, so you're spread out automatically.
Cash: safe and steady, but can lose value to inflation.

body.text: Before you invest

items: Clear expensive debt first (credit cards, overdrafts).
Build an emergency fund in cash.
Only invest money you won't need for at least 5 years.
Use a tax wrapper (Stocks & Shares ISA, or a pension).

body.text: Principles that matter most

items: Diversify: spread across many companies and countries.
Keep costs low: fees compound against you.
Time in the market beats timing the market.
Don't panic-sell in a crash. Selling locks in the loss.

body.text: Be wary of apps that make trading feel like a game (confetti, leaderboards, constant alerts). The FCA has warned these features can push people into riskier, more frequent trading.
This is education, not personal advice. If you're unsure, MoneyHelper offers free guidance.

articles.title: Funds, platforms & fees
articles.summary: Index funds, platform and fund fees, and why small percentages matter.

body.text: Fees look tiny as percentages, but they're taken every year and compound against you.
The fees you'll see

items: Fund fee (ongoing charges figure, OCF): the yearly cost of running the fund.
Platform fee: what the app or broker charges to hold your investments.
Dealing fees: per buy or sell, on some platforms.
FX fees: when buying assets priced in other currencies.
Over decades, high fees can eat a large share of your growth

body.text: Index funds and ETFs

Index funds and ETFs track a market (like a global stock index) instead of paying managers to pick winners. That usually means lower fees and broad diversification, which is why many beginners start there.
Accumulation vs income
Accumulation units reinvest dividends automatically. Income units pay them out. For long-term growth, accumulation keeps your money compounding.
Compare platforms by total yearly cost for YOUR pot size. Flat fees suit bigger pots, percentage fees suit smaller ones.

articles.title: Free share offers
articles.summary: How free-share sign-up offers work and the terms to check.

body.text: Some trading apps give you a free share, or cash to invest, when you sign up or refer a friend. It can be a nice bonus, but it's still an investment.
Check before you sign up

items: Is the firm authorised? Check the FCA Register.
Minimum deposit or holding period before you can sell or withdraw.
The range of possible share values. Most people get the lower end.
Fees once the promotion ends.
Whether the account is a Stocks & Shares ISA or a taxable account.

body.text: The value of the share can fall. Don't deposit more than you're comfortable investing just to unlock a bonus.
Treat the free share as a way to learn how a platform works, not as a reason to start trading frequently.

articles.title: Compound growth
articles.summary: The maths of growth, the Rule of 72 and regular investing.

body.text: Compounding means your growth earns growth. Over long periods it's the most powerful force in personal finance, for savings and for debt.

items: £2,000 growing 7% a year becomes about £3,930 in 10 years
£100 a month at 5% for 30 years grows to about £83,000 (you pay in £36,000)
Rule of 72: years to double ≈ 72 ÷ growth rate

body.text: Start early

Two people invest £100 a month at 6% until 65. The one who starts at 25 ends up with far more than the one who starts at 35, much more than the extra £12,000 paid in, because of 10 extra years of compounding.
Falls hurt more than you think
If an investment falls 50%, it needs to rise 100% to get back to where it was. A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall leaves you down 1%. That's why diversification and staying invested matter.
Regular investing
Investing a fixed amount every month (pound-cost averaging) means you automatically buy more when prices are low and less when they're high, without trying to predict the market.
Compounding works against you on debt too: a credit card balance at 24% roughly doubles in 3 years if you don't pay it.

articles.title: Crypto: the risks
articles.summary: Volatility, no FSCS protection and common crypto scams.

body.text: Crypto assets can swing wildly in value, and they have far fewer protections than savings or regulated investments.
The key risks

items: Extreme volatility: prices can fall 50% or more quickly.
No FSCS protection if an exchange fails.
No Financial Ombudsman route for many complaints.
Scams are common: fake exchanges, “pump” groups, fake celebrity ads and romance scams.

body.text: If you choose to buy

items: Only use money you could afford to lose entirely.
Use firms registered with the FCA for crypto activities, and check the FCA Warning List.
Never share wallet recovery phrases. Anyone with them owns your crypto.
Be suspicious of anyone who contacted you first or promises returns.

body.text: Anyone asking you to pay in crypto, whether a “bank”, “HMRC” or an “investment manager”, is almost certainly a scammer.

articles.title: Your tax-free allowances
articles.summary: Personal Allowance, savings and dividend allowances, and the tax year.

body.text: Everyone has tax-free allowances. Knowing them helps you keep more of your money, and choose between savings, ISAs and investments.

items: Personal Allowance: £12,570 of income tax-free (reduced by £1 for every £2 earned over £100,000)
Personal Savings Allowance: £1,000 of interest tax-free for basic-rate taxpayers, £500 for higher-rate, £0 for additional-rate
Dividend allowance: £500
Capital Gains Tax annual exempt amount: £3,000
ISAs: everything inside is tax-free, on top of these allowances

body.text: The tax year
The UK tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April. Allowances reset each year, and most can't be carried forward.
Your tax code

Your tax code tells your employer how much tax-free pay you get. A new job can mean an emergency code and too much tax for a while. Check your personal tax account on gov.uk, and HMRC will refund any overpayment once it's corrected.
Keep your P60 (yearly pay and tax summary). You'll need it for mortgages, refunds and claims.
Tax rates and allowances change in Budgets. Figures are for 2026/27, checked October 2026.

articles.title: Side income & HMRC
articles.summary: The trading allowance, selling your own stuff, platform reporting and Self Assessment.

body.text: Side income is great, but HMRC needs to know about it once it's above certain limits.

items: Trading allowance: £1,000 of gross side income a year without telling HMRC
Property allowance: £1,000 of property income
Rent a Room: up to £7,500 a year tax-free for letting a furnished room in your own home
Self Assessment online deadline: 31 January after the tax year ends

body.text: Selling your own stuff
Clearing out your own belongings isn't trading, and isn't normally taxed. Buying things to resell for profit is trading.
Platform reporting

Online marketplaces now share details with HMRC once someone sells 30 or more items, or about £1,700 or more, in a year. Being reported doesn't automatically mean you owe tax. It depends on whether you're trading.
Over the allowance?

items: Register for Self Assessment by 5 October after the tax year you started.
Keep records of income and allowable expenses.
File and pay by 31 January. A late return means an automatic £100 penalty, even if no tax is owed.

body.text: If your combined self-employed and property income is over £50,000, Making Tax Digital rules (quarterly digital updates) started applying from April 2026.
Rules depend on your situation. Use gov.uk's checkers, or speak to an accountant if your side income is growing.

articles.title: Marriage Allowance
articles.summary: Transferring allowance between partners.

body.text: If you're married or in a civil partnership, and one of you earns less than the Personal Allowance, you may be able to transfer some allowance and save tax.

items: Transfer £1,260 of Personal Allowance to your partner
Saves up to £252 a year
Can be backdated up to 4 years

body.text: Who qualifies

items: The lower earner has income below the Personal Allowance (£12,570).
The higher earner is a basic-rate taxpayer.
You're married or in a civil partnership.

body.text: How to apply
Apply for free on gov.uk. You don't need a company to do it for you. Some firms charge a cut of your refund for something you can do in minutes.

articles.title: Your credit score
articles.summary: Hard vs soft searches, utilisation, the electoral roll and how long things stay on file.

body.text: Your credit file is your borrowing history, held by credit reference agencies (Experian, Equifax and TransUnion). Lenders use it to decide whether to lend to you and at what rate. Each agency's “score” is its own estimate. Lenders make their own decisions.
Check it for free

You have a legal right to see your credit file for free, and all three agencies offer free access through their own or partner services. Checking your own file is a soft search and never affects your score.
What helps

items: Being on the electoral roll at your current address.
Paying everything on time. Set up at least minimum-payment Direct Debits.
Keeping credit card balances low compared with your limits (low utilisation).
A long, steady history: older accounts managed well.
Using eligibility checkers before applying (they use soft searches).

body.text: What hurts

items: Missed or late payments, defaults and CCJs. These usually stay on your file for six years.
Lots of applications in a short time (hard searches are visible to lenders, usually for about a year).
Maxed-out cards.
Financial links to someone with poor credit through joint accounts or loans.

body.text: Spot something wrong on your file? Ask the agency to correct it. Mistakes are more common than you'd think.

articles.title: Credit cards done right
articles.summary: Paying in full, Section 75, chargeback and 0% deals.

body.text: Used well, a credit card can give you protection, rewards and a stronger credit file. Used badly, it's some of the most expensive borrowing there is. The difference is whether you pay in full.
The golden rule
Set up a Direct Debit to pay the full balance every month. Then you usually pay no interest on purchases and still get the benefits.
Section 75 protection

Pay for something costing between £100 and £30,000, even partly, on a credit card, and the card provider is jointly responsible if it goes wrong (faulty, not delivered, firm goes bust). For debit cards, and items under £100, ask your bank about chargeback instead.
0% deals

items: 0% purchase cards: spread a big cost interest-free. Clear it before the deal ends.
0% balance transfer cards: move expensive debt to 0%. There's usually a one-off fee (often a few percent).
Example: £3,000 moved with a 3% fee for 20 months costs £3,090, so £154.50 a month clears it in time.
When the 0% ends, the normal rate applies to whatever's left.

body.text: Avoid cash withdrawals on credit cards. They usually charge a fee plus interest from day one.

articles.title: The true cost of borrowing
articles.summary: APR, minimum payments, payday loans and guarantor loans.

body.text: Before you borrow, compare the total cost, not just the monthly payment.
APR
The APR includes interest and compulsory fees as a yearly rate, so you can compare offers. Advertised “representative” APRs only need to be given to most applicants. Your rate could be higher.
Minimum payments

items: £1,000 at about 24% APR, paying a fixed £25 a month, takes around 6 years to clear
It costs roughly £750 in interest
Paying a bit more each month makes a big difference

body.text: Common borrowing, cheapest to dearest (usually)

items: 0% card deals cleared in time.
Personal loans (for good credit, larger amounts).
Credit cards with interest, and arranged overdrafts.
Store cards and catalogue credit.
Payday loans: capped by the FCA, but still among the most expensive.

body.text: Car finance (PCP)
With PCP you pay monthly, then either hand the car back, pay a large final “balloon” payment to keep it, or part-exchange. You don't own the car unless you pay the balloon.
Guarantor loans
Someone else promises to repay if you can't. It can strain relationships, so only agree if you're able and willing to pay.
Struggling to repay? Talk to your lender early. It must help customers in financial difficulty. Free debt advice: StepChange, Citizens Advice, MoneyHelper.

articles.title: Buy Now Pay Later
articles.summary: How BNPL works and how to avoid its traps.

body.text: Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) splits a purchase into instalments, often interest-free. It feels painless, which is exactly why it's easy to overdo.

items: Agreements taken out from 15 July 2026 are regulated by the FCA
Lenders must check you can afford it
You can complain to the Financial Ombudsman, and Section 75 refunds may apply
Agreements from before that date are not covered

body.text: The risks

items: Stacking several plans at once and losing track.
Late fees, and missed payments being passed to debt collectors.
Missed payments can affect your credit file.
Spending more than you would with money you actually have.

body.text: Use it safely

items: Only use BNPL for things you could afford to pay for today.
Keep a list of every plan and its payment dates.
Pay from an account that always has the money in it.
Avoid BNPL for everyday essentials. If you need it for food, talk to a free debt adviser.

articles.title: Renting in England: your rights since 1 May 2026
articles.summary: What changed under the Renters' Rights Act, and what it means for you as a tenant.

body.text: Most changes from the Renters' Rights Act 2025 started on 1 May 2026. This guide covers England only. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have their own rules.

items: Landlords can no longer end a tenancy with a 'no fault' section 21 notice.
New tenancies are rolling (periodic) with no fixed end date. Existing assured shorthold tenancies became periodic tenancies on 1 May 2026.
You can leave by giving 2 months' written notice, on the rent day or the day before.
A landlord who wants you out needs a legal ground and usually gives 4 months' notice, though some grounds allow less.

body.text: Rent increases

Rent can go up once a year, and not in the first 12 months. The landlord must use the official form (Form 4A) and give at least 2 months' notice. You can challenge an increase that is above market rent.
Finding a place

items: Adverts and offers must state a specific price. Landlords cannot accept or encourage offers above the advertised rent.
Landlords cannot ask for or accept rent before the tenancy agreement is signed. After signing, they can ask for at most 1 month's rent in advance.
You can ask to keep a pet. The landlord must consider it and give a reason if they refuse.
Landlords cannot refuse to rent to you because you receive benefits or have children.

body.text: If something goes wrong

Councils have new powers to act against landlords who break the rules. For some offences, such as renting out a property that should be licensed, tenants can apply to the First-tier Tribunal for a Rent Repayment Order, which can require repayment of up to 2 years' rent.
Keep your tenancy agreement, rent receipts and messages with your landlord. They are your evidence if there is a dispute.
This is general information, not legal advice. If you are facing eviction or a dispute, contact Shelter, Citizens Advice or your council. Rules and dates can change, so check the gov.uk pages below.

articles.title: Deposits and fees: what a landlord can charge
articles.summary: The legal limits on holding deposits, tenancy deposits and other charges in England.

body.text: In England, landlords and agents can only charge the payments the law allows. Anything else is a banned fee.

items: Rent.
A tenancy deposit, capped at 5 weeks' rent (6 weeks if the annual rent is £50,000 or more).
A holding deposit, capped at 1 week's rent.
Damages for breaking the tenancy agreement.
Reasonable fees to change or leave the tenancy, and to replace a lost key.
Council tax, utilities, communications and TV licence, if the agreement says you pay them.

body.text: Holding deposits

Only one holding deposit can be taken for a property at a time. Usually the deadline to agree the tenancy is the 15th day after the landlord agrees to the deposit, unless you both agree another date in writing. If the tenancy goes ahead, or the landlord decides not to proceed, the holding deposit must usually be returned within 7 days. A landlord can keep it only in set cases, such as false or misleading information, and must give written reasons within 7 days.
Your tenancy deposit must be protected

items: The landlord or agent must protect your deposit in a government-approved scheme within 30 days of receiving it.
They must give you the prescribed information about where it is held.
You can ask the scheme to confirm your deposit is protected.
If it was not protected properly, you may be able to claim compensation through the County Court.

body.text: Banned fees and limits

items: Reference check fees and other charges for granting a tenancy are banned.
A late-rent fee is only allowed once rent is at least 14 days overdue, and is capped at 3% above the Bank of England base rate on the unpaid amount.
Fees for changing the tenancy are capped at £50 unless the landlord can justify higher reasonable costs.
Councils can fine landlords up to £5,000 for a first breach, and up to £30,000 for a repeat breach within 5 years.

body.text: Ask for fees to be listed in writing before you pay anything. Pay by a method you can prove, such as bank transfer, and keep receipts.
General information for England, not legal advice. Check the limits with Shelter or your council before paying a disputed charge.

articles.title: Paying your rent on time
articles.summary: Ways to pay, keeping proof, and what to do if you cannot pay.

body.text: Paying rent on time protects your home, and keeps late fees and disputes away. A little set-up makes it automatic.
Ways to pay

items: Standing order: you set it up with your bank, with a fixed amount on a fixed date.
Direct Debit: set up by the landlord or agent, who collects the payment. Make sure you know how to cancel it with your bank.
Bank transfer: manual, so put a reminder in your calendar a few days before the due date.

body.text: Make it easy to prove

items: Pay from an account in your own name.
Use the reference your landlord gives you.
Keep bank statements or receipts for the whole tenancy.
Report repairs and ask about problems in writing.

body.text: Late fees
Landlords can only charge a late-rent fee when rent is at least 14 days overdue, and the amount is capped. It cannot be a flat penalty fee.
If you cannot pay

Tell your landlord or agent as early as you can. Ask what they can agree in writing. Free, independent help is available from Shelter, Citizens Advice and MoneyHelper, and your council may be able to help too. Do not ignore letters about arrears.
Check your tenancy agreement for who pays council tax and utilities. Budget for them with your rent.
General information, not advice. Rules differ in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

articles.title: Can your rent help your credit file?
articles.summary: How rent reporting works, what it costs, and why it is not a sure thing.

body.text: Normally, paying rent does not appear on your credit file. Rent reporting services aim to change that, so lenders can see you pay on time. It can help if you have a thin credit history, but it is not guaranteed to raise your score.

items: A service such as CreditLadder asks for read-only access to your bank transactions through Open Banking, finds your rent payments, and reports them to credit reference agencies.
As reviewed by Finder in November 2023, reporting to one agency was free, and reporting to all four cost £5 to £8 a month. Prices may have changed, so check the provider.
Lenders do not have to use rent data, and many do not. Any score change can take months and is not guaranteed.
You can pay rent from an account the service supports. If your landlord refers you to a service, you can decline.

body.text: Other routes
Some landlords report to Experian's Rental Exchange. Credit-builder products, and being on the electoral roll, can also help. Check which route suits you before paying for anything.
Risks

items: Missing rent payments can lead to arrears and, in the worst case, a court judgment, which is recorded for six years unless paid in full within 30 days.
Paying a monthly fee only to see your own rent payments is not worth it if no lender you use looks at the data.

body.text: Ask the lender you are applying to whether they use rent data before paying for reporting.
General information, not financial advice. Check the provider's current terms and fees. This guide does not recommend any service.

articles.title: Rent rewards: ways to pay rent and get something back
articles.summary: The UK rent-rewards services compared on rate, fees and catches, with a worked example.

body.text: A few UK services let you pay rent and earn points or cashback. The rewards are usually small, and the terms change often, so work out the real value before you switch how you pay your rent. Details below were checked on 13 October 2026, partly from the providers' own pages and partly from third-party reviews.
Services that pay your landlord for you

items: Ribbon Rewards: you transfer rent into an account in your name, and Ribbon sends it to your landlord or agent on rent day. Its page says it earns 1 point per £1 of rent, with 100 points = £1 in vouchers, so about 1% in vouchers. It lists a higher 'up to 3 points per £1' rate as coming soon. It says the service is free, accounts are provided by Griffin Bank, and eligible deposits are protected by the FSCS up to £120,000. An optional Credit Builder add-on costs £7.99 to £9.99 a month.

Rentd: an app and debit card. A press release from 1 September 2026 says all tiers earn 1 point per £1 on rent, with boosted points on everyday spending if you hit a monthly spend target. One review (updated 24 September 2026) says 5,000 points now buy a £25 gift card, which is about 0.5p a point, so about 0.5% on rent. Topping up by credit card costs 1.95%. Rentd's own page did not give these figures when I checked, so confirm the current value in the app.

Yonder, Brick Rewards and Renti Rewards: other services that earn points on rent. Reviews describe different ways of earning, for example Open Banking for Brick Rewards, and 1 point per £1 for Renti Rewards. Rates, conversion values and eligibility were not clear, so check each provider's terms.

body.text: Paying rent by credit card

Services such as Nuba take a card payment and pay your landlord by bank transfer. A January 2026 review lists fees of 1.99% for Visa and Mastercard and 2.49% for American Express. On £1,000 of rent that is £19.90 or £24.90. It only makes sense if your card rewards are worth more than the fee, for example to reach a sign-up bonus spend target. Payments through such services can be final and non-refundable, and a chargeback can still leave you owing the service.
A worked example

items: £1,000 a month rent, paid through Ribbon at 1 point per £1 and 100 points = £1: about £10 a month, £120 a year, in vouchers.
The same rent at Rentd at 1 point per £1 and 5,000 points = £25: about £5 a month, £60 a year, if that conversion is still current.
The same rent by credit card through a service charging 1.99%: a £19.90 fee a month. Card rewards would have to beat that.

body.text: What to check before you switch

items: Is the value in cash, vouchers or points, and can you actually spend it on things you buy anyway?
Does the service hold your money, and is it protected (for example by the FSCS)?
Does your tenancy agreement or landlord need to know your new payment details? Tell them and keep proof the rent arrived on time.
Are there fees, tier spend targets or expiry dates?
Do any rewards depend on a referral or sign-up bonus that has conditions?

body.text: Paying rent late can lead to arrears and, in serious cases, loss of your home. A reward is never worth a missed payment, so keep a buffer and leave extra time for transfers. Rates and terms change often. This is general information, not financial advice. Some of the sources are referral-supported.
Put the real numbers into 'Is this offer worth my time?' in Tools before you switch.

articles.title: Paying rent by credit card: read this first
articles.summary: Services that let you pay rent by card, the fees, and the risks.

body.text: Some services now let tenants pay rent with a credit card, while the landlord still receives a normal bank transfer. People do it to earn rewards or to spread the cost. It only makes sense if the numbers work and you can repay in full.

items: Services usually charge a fee. Compare it with any rewards you could earn.
If you do not clear the card balance in full by the due date, interest can cost more than the rewards.
Rent is a large, regular payment. Card limits and your credit utilisation can be affected.
Landlords may not accept card payments directly, so you would use a service in between.

body.text: Before you try it

items: Work out the total fee over a year.
Check what the card pays in rewards and whether rent counts.
Make sure you can repay in full every month.
Read the service's terms, and keep proof that the landlord received the rent.

body.text: Paying rent late can lead to arrears and, in serious cases, loss of your home. Never put rent on a card you cannot clear. This is general information, not financial advice.
Use the 'Is this offer worth my time?' tool in Tools to put the fee and reward side by side.

articles.title: Budgeting basics
articles.summary: 50/30/20, needs vs wants, pay yourself first and zero-based budgets.

body.text: A budget is just a plan for your money before it arrives, so it goes where you want instead of disappearing. It doesn't need to be complicated.
Start with take-home pay
Budget with what actually lands in your account after tax, National Insurance, pension and student loan deductions, not your headline salary.
Three simple methods

items: 50/30/20: roughly 50% needs (rent, bills, food, transport), 30% wants, 20% savings or extra debt payments. On £2,000 take-home, that's £1,000 / £600 / £400.
Pots or envelopes: split money into separate pots for bills, food, fun and savings. Most banking apps support this.
Zero-based: give every pound a job until nothing is unassigned, including savings.

body.text: If your needs are well over 50% (common with London rents), don't panic. Use the split as a direction, not a rule.
Pay yourself first
Set an automatic transfer to savings on payday. Saving whatever's left at the end of the month rarely works.
If you have debts

items: Avalanche: pay minimums on everything, then put extra money on the highest interest rate first. This saves the most money.
Snowball: put extra on the smallest balance first. Quick wins keep you motivated.
Either beats doing nothing. Pick the one you'll stick to.

body.text: If you can't cover essentials or minimum payments, get free help now from StepChange, Citizens Advice or MoneyHelper. Never pay for debt advice.
Small leaks add up
£5 a day is about £1,825 a year. Track your spending for one month. Most people are surprised where the money goes.

articles.title: Subscription clear-out
articles.summary: Finding and cancelling forgotten subscriptions.

body.text: Forgotten subscriptions are one of the easiest savings you'll ever find. A single £12.99 monthly subscription costs £155.88 a year.
The 20-minute clear-out

items: Open your banking app and search for recurring payments (many apps list them).
Check your app store subscriptions on your phone too.
List each one: cost per month, last time you used it.
Cancel anything you haven't used in the last month.
Downgrade or share plans where allowed. Rotate streaming services month by month instead of holding them all.

body.text: Free trial traps

items: Read the price after the trial and how to cancel before you enter card details.
Set a reminder a day before the trial ends.
Be wary of trials that can only be cancelled by phone during office hours.

body.text: Once a year, call your providers (phone, broadband, insurance) and ask for a better deal. Many will offer one to keep you.

articles.title: Saving goals
articles.summary: SMART goals and sinking funds.

body.text: Goals turn saving from a chore into a plan. The trick is making them specific and automatic.
Make it SMART
Not “save more” but “save £600 for a holiday by June by putting away £100 a month”. Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

items: £6,000 in 2 years = £250 a month
£1,200 in 12 months = £100 a month
£500 starter emergency fund in 10 weeks = £50 a week

body.text: Sinking funds for the predictable stuff

Car insurance, MOT, Christmas, birthdays and annual subscriptions aren't emergencies, because you know they're coming. Divide each yearly cost by 12 and save that monthly in a separate pot, and they'll never hit you as a shock.
Make progress visible

items: Name your savings pots after the goal.
Round-ups and automatic transfers do the work for you.
Put windfalls (bonuses, cashback payouts, switch bonuses) straight towards a goal.

articles.title: Unit prices & real value
articles.summary: Price per kg/litre, multipacks, offers and shrinkflation.

body.text: The shelf price tells you what you pay. The unit price (per kg, litre, 100g or item) tells you what's actually good value.

items: 6 eggs for £1.50 = 25p each; 15 for £3.30 = 22p each
4-pack of tins for £4.00 = £1 a tin; a single tin at 95p is cheaper
“3 for 2” on £3.60 bottles = £7.20 for three

body.text: Traps to watch

items: Multipacks that cost more per unit than singles.
Shrinkflation: smaller pack, same price.
“Up to 70% off”, where only a few items get the full discount.
Buy-one-get-one-free on things you'll throw away before using.

body.text: Simple habits

items: Read the small unit price on the shelf label, not just the big price.
Compare own-brand with branded, and do a blind taste test at home.
Shop later in the day for yellow-sticker reductions on things you'll eat soon.
Use price-match promises where shops offer them.

articles.title: Supermarket stacking
articles.summary: Gift cards, cashback cards and loyalty points on one shop.

body.text: Stacking means layering several savings on the same shop. Each layer is small, but together they add up every week.
The layers

items: Buy a supermarket gift card through a cashback or gift card app (often a few percent back).
Pay for that gift card with a cashback debit or credit card, if you have one.
Pay for your shop with the gift card.
Scan your loyalty card as normal. Points are earned separately.
£50 gift card at 4% off = £2, plus 50 loyalty points (50p) = £2.50 saved
On a £100 weekly shop, a 5% stack is about £260 a year

body.text: Rules for stacking safely

items: Only buy gift cards for shops you definitely use, for roughly the amount you'll spend soon.
Compare rates across apps before buying. They change often.
If paying by credit card, clear it in full so interest doesn't wipe out the saving.
Keep gift card balances low. If a retailer collapses, unused balances can be lost.

body.text: Live gift card and cashback offers are in the Money Hunters app, with the date each was last checked.

articles.title: Loyalty schemes
articles.summary: Getting the most from points.

body.text: Loyalty points are a small discount you've already earned. The trick is spending them where they're worth most, and not letting them expire.
Getting more from points

items: Check partner rewards. Points can be worth more with partners (restaurants, days out, travel) than at the till.
Watch for points multipliers on things you buy anyway.
Use member prices, but compare them with competitors. A “member price” isn't always the cheapest.
Check expiry rules and use points before they lapse.
1,000 points = £10 at the till, or £30 with a partner = three times the value

body.text: Don't buy things you don't need just to earn points. 10% back on a purchase you didn't need is still 90% spent.

articles.title: Your consumer rights
articles.summary: Refunds, faulty goods and cooling-off periods.

body.text: When you buy from a business, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 gives you rights. You don't need a receipt for these rights to exist, but you do need proof of purchase.

items: Faulty goods: full refund within 30 days
Within 6 months: the seller must repair or replace, and it's assumed the fault was there from the start
Online and phone purchases: usually 14 days to cancel (cooling-off), with some exceptions

body.text: Your rights in plain English

items: Goods must be of satisfactory quality, fit for purpose and as described.
Services must be carried out with reasonable care and skill.
Refurbished and second-hand goods from a trader still carry rights, allowing for their age and condition.
Personalised items, perishables and unsealed hygiene items are usually excluded from the 14-day cooling-off.

body.text: Extra protection when you pay
Credit card purchases of £100 to £30,000 may be covered by Section 75. Debit card purchases may be recoverable through chargeback.
Extended warranties at the checkout are often poor value. Check what the law and the manufacturer already cover first.

articles.title: Cashback sites
articles.summary: How cashback sites work and how to get paid.

body.text: Cashback sites earn a commission when you buy through their link, and pass part of it to you. Used on things you were already buying, it's free money.
How to use them

items: Sign up to one or two major cashback sites.
Before buying online, search for the shop on the cashback site and compare rates (they differ).
Click through from the cashback site, then buy as normal.
Check that the cashback appears as “pending”.
Withdraw it once it's “payable”, to your bank or as a gift card.
£400 laptop: 3% cashback + 1% cashback card = £16 back
Insurance, broadband and energy often pay the biggest cashback

body.text: Cashback can take weeks or months to confirm, and it can be declined. Don't count it until it's paid.
Never buy something just for the cashback. Use it to make planned purchases cheaper.

articles.title: Making cashback track
articles.summary: Cookies, ad blockers, voucher codes and declined cashback.

body.text: Most missing cashback comes down to tracking. The cashback site needs to see that your purchase came from its link.
Make it track

items: Start from the cashback site every time, and complete the purchase in the same session.
Accept cookies, and pause ad blockers and coupon or price extensions.
Don't jump to price comparison or voucher sites in between.
Use the cashback site's app or browser extension if it has one.

body.text: Why cashback gets declined

items: Returning or cancelling the order.
Using a voucher code not listed on the cashback site.
Excluded products, delivery charges or gift cards.
Being an existing customer when the offer is for new customers only.

body.text: Voucher vs cashback
A 10% voucher on £120 saves £12 now, while 8% cashback is £9.60 later. Take the bigger, more certain saving.
Screenshot your order confirmation. If cashback doesn't track, most sites let you file a missing cashback claim.

articles.title: Gift card cashback apps
articles.summary: Discounted gift cards and their risks.

body.text: Gift card apps sell retailer gift cards at a discount or with cashback. You then spend the card as normal and keep the saving.
Best practice

items: Check the cashback rate for your shop just before you buy, as rates move.
Buy only the amount you'll spend soon.
Pay with a card that also earns rewards, but clear any credit card in full.
Spend the gift card, and withdraw the cashback from the app regularly.

body.text: Risks

items: Unused balances can be lost if a retailer goes into administration.
Some gift cards expire. Check the date.
Gift cards are rarely refundable once bought.

body.text: Anyone who asks you to pay a bill, fine or tax in gift cards is a scammer. No real organisation does this.

articles.title: Phishing texts & emails
articles.summary: Spotting fake messages and links.

body.text: Phishing is a fake text, email or call designed to get your details or your money. It's the most common way scams start, and once you know the pattern, they become easy to spot.
The 6 red flags

items: Urgency: “within 24 hours”, “account locked”, “final notice”.
Surprise money: refunds, rebates and prizes you didn't expect.
Links to lookalike addresses (e.g. a “gov-uk-refund” site rather than one ending in gov.uk).
Requests for card details, passwords, PINs or one-time codes.
Generic greetings: “Dear Customer”.
Odd payment methods: gift cards, crypto, bank transfer to a personal account.

body.text: Safe habits

items: Never use the link or number in an unexpected message.
Open the official app, or type the address yourself.
Check delivery, tax and bank issues inside your real accounts.
If in doubt, ask someone you trust. Scammers rely on you acting alone and fast.

body.text: A padlock in the browser only means the connection is encrypted. Scam sites can have padlocks too.
Play the Daily Mystery and Scam of the Day in the game. Spotting flags becomes automatic with practice.

articles.title: Bank impersonation & APP fraud
articles.summary: Safe-account scams, 159, and reimbursement rules.

body.text: In Authorised Push Payment (APP) fraud, you're tricked into sending money yourself, often by someone pretending to be your bank, the police, a seller or a loved one.
Things your bank will never do

items: Ask you to move money to a “safe account”.
Ask for your full PIN, password or a one-time code.
Ask you to install remote-access apps.
Ask you to keep a call secret, even from branch staff.
Pressure you to act immediately.

body.text: If someone calls claiming to be your bank

items: Hang up. Caller ID can be faked (“spoofing”).
Call 159 (it connects you to many UK banks), or the number on the back of your card.
Use a different phone if you can, or wait 5 minutes, because some scammers keep the line open.

body.text: If you've already paid

items: Call your bank immediately. Speed matters.
Report it to Report Fraud, the national service (it replaced Action Fraud in December 2025).
Keep all messages, numbers and receipts.
Banks must reimburse most APP fraud victims up to £85,000 per claim
Claims within 13 months of the last payment
An excess of up to £100 may apply (not for vulnerable customers)
Covers UK Faster Payments and CHAPS made from 7 October 2024

body.text: You could lose protection if you ignore clear warnings or are found to be grossly negligent, so take bank warnings seriously.

articles.title: Investment & crypto scams
articles.summary: Guaranteed returns, fake platforms and recovery scams.

body.text: Investment scams cause some of the biggest losses because they look professional and promise a lot. They come as social media ads, WhatsApp groups, cold calls and fake apps.
Warning signs

items: Guaranteed or very high returns (“10% a month, no risk”).
Fake celebrity endorsements in ads.
Pressure to decide today, or “only a few places left”.
Payment in crypto, or to a personal account.
“Mentors” in group chats, and apps that show big profits but won't let you withdraw without paying a fee.
Unexpected calls about pensions. Pension cold calling is illegal in the UK.

body.text: Clone firms
Scammers copy the name, address and registration number of real authorised firms. Check the FCA Register, and only contact a firm using the details listed there, not the ones they give you.
Before you invest a penny

items: Check the firm on the FCA Register and the FCA Warning List.
Use the FCA's ScamSmart checker.
Never invest through someone who contacted you out of the blue.
Talk to MoneyHelper (free) about pensions.

body.text: “Recovery” firms that contact you after a scam, offering to get your money back for a fee, are usually a second scam.

articles.title: Shopping & marketplace scams
articles.summary: Fake shops, tickets and marketplace tricks.

body.text: Shopping scams take your money for goods or tickets that never arrive, or take the goods without paying. They thrive on bargains and unprotected payments.
Buying

items: Prices far below normal are the bait.
Sellers who refuse PayPal Goods & Services or card payments, and want bank transfer or “Friends & Family”.
Sellers who can't meet you (“I'm working abroad, a courier will deliver”).
New accounts with no history, especially for tickets.
Pets and holiday rentals you can't see before paying.

body.text: Selling

items: Buyers who send you a link to “receive payment” and ask for your card details.
Overpayments with a request to refund the difference.
Fake “escrow” services the buyer insists on.
Never hand over goods until the money has cleared in your own account.

body.text: Your protection

Paying by credit card can give you Section 75 protection for purchases between £100 and £30,000. Debit cards can use chargeback. Bank transfers have the least protection, although APP fraud reimbursement may help.
Check fake shops: look up reviews and company details, and be wary of free email addresses and “pay by bank transfer for extra discount”.

articles.title: Job scams & money mules
articles.summary: Task scams, fake jobs and money muling.

body.text: Job scams target people looking for extra income. Some steal your money, and some trick you into committing crimes.
Task scams
You're paid small amounts to like videos or rate products, then asked to “top up” to unlock bigger tasks or withdraw. The balance is fake. Paying to earn is always a scam.
Money mules

A “payments assistant” or “parcel reshipping” job that moves money or goods through your account or address is money laundering. Mules can be prosecuted, lose their bank accounts and struggle to get credit for years, even if they didn't realise what was happening.
Fake recruiters

items: Unsolicited offers on WhatsApp or Telegram.
Interviews by text chat only.
Requests for your passport and bank details before any real offer.
Cheques sent to you with a request to send part of the money on.

body.text: Real employers interview you, don't charge you, and never ask you to move money for them.

articles.title: Reporting scams & staying secure
articles.summary: 7726, phishing reports, passwords and 2FA.

body.text: Reporting scams helps block them for everyone, and doing it fast can help you get money back.

items: Scam text: forward it to 7726 (free)
Scam email: forward it to report@phishing.gov.uk
Suspicious call about your bank: hang up and call 159
Fraud or cyber crime: Report Fraud (reportfraud.police.uk, 0300 123 2040)
Lost money: call your bank immediately

body.text: Lock your accounts down

items: Use a different password for every important account. A password manager makes it easy.
Turn on two-step verification (2FA) for email, banking and social media.
Never share one-time codes, even with “friends”: their account may be hacked.
Keep your phone and apps updated.
Freeze your card in your banking app if you lose it.

body.text: Your email account is the master key: it can reset every other password. Protect it first.

articles.title: Survey sites
articles.summary: What they pay, screen-outs and red flags.

body.text: Survey sites pay small amounts for your opinions. They're good for idle minutes, but they're not an income.

items: Typical pay: a few pence to a couple of pounds per survey
Expect “screen-outs” when you're not the audience
Check the minimum cash-out before you start

body.text: Make it worth your time

items: Fill in your profile honestly, so you get matched to more surveys and fewer screen-outs.
Work out your hourly rate. £1 for 10 minutes is £6 an hour, and £2.50 for 30 minutes is only £5.
Stick to a few well-reviewed sites.

body.text: Real survey sites are free. Paying to join, or to “unlock” higher-paying surveys, is a red flag. Never give bank details to claim a survey prize.

articles.title: Reward & game apps
articles.summary: Play-to-earn milestones, cash-outs and hourly rates.

body.text: Reward and game apps pay you in points for playing, shopping or completing tasks. Some are fun extras, some are a big time sink, and some are scams.
Before you start

items: What are the points worth in £, and what's the minimum cash-out?
For game offers: what level by what deadline? Missing it by a day usually means nothing.
Recent payout reviews from real users.
£15 for reaching level 30 in 14 days, taking about 25 hours = 60p an hour
1,000 points = £1, earning 2,000 points an hour = £2 an hour

body.text: Red flags

items: Paying to withdraw or “unlock VIP” earnings.
“Task” apps asking you to top up a balance.
Unrealistic daily earnings.

body.text: Multi-level marketing
MLM schemes recruit you to sell products and recruit others. Studies and regulators have found most participants earn little or lose money after costs.

articles.title: Selling your stuff
articles.summary: Getting the best price and staying safe.

body.text: Selling things you no longer need is one of the quickest ways to raise cash, and selling your own belongings usually isn't taxed.
Sell faster, for more

items: Price it using recently SOLD listings, not asking prices.
Take clear photos in daylight from several angles.
Write an honest description, including flaws.
Compare postage options, or offer local collection.
Reply quickly and be polite. Good reviews help you sell again.

body.text: Stay safe

items: Only accept payment inside the platform, or in cash when meeting.
Never click a buyer's link to “receive payment”.
Never refund an “overpayment”.
Meet in public places for collections.

body.text: If you start buying things to resell for profit, that's trading. Check the £1,000 trading allowance and HMRC rules.

articles.title: Referral programmes
articles.summary: How referrals work and how to share codes honestly.

body.text: Referral schemes reward you, and often your friend, when someone signs up through your link or code. Done honestly, everyone wins.
Doing it right

items: Only refer people to things you'd genuinely recommend.
Tell people it's a referral link.
Read the terms on both sides: who gets what, and the conditions.
Respect community rules. Many forums and subreddits ban referral links.

body.text: Fake or duplicate accounts to claim referral bonuses break the terms, can be fraud, and lead to clawbacks or bans.
Money Hunters may earn from some referral links. It never changes the offer you get, and the game never rewards you for signing up to anything.

articles.title: Energy bills
articles.summary: The price cap, standing charges and switching.

body.text: Energy bills are made of two parts: a daily standing charge, and a unit rate for each kWh you use.
The price cap
Ofgem sets a price cap on standard variable tariffs, reviewed every quarter. It caps the unit rates and standing charges, not your total bill. Use more and you pay more.
Fixed vs variable

items: Fixed: your rates are locked for a term (your bill still depends on usage). Exit fees may apply.
Variable (default): rates move with the price cap.

body.text: Switching
Switching supplier doesn't interrupt your supply. It's the same pipes and wires. Compare fixed deals against the current cap before you sign.
Cut usage

items: Pay by monthly Direct Debit (usually cheaper).
Submit regular meter readings, or use a smart meter.
Turn devices off at the wall rather than standby.
Check your boiler flow temperature and draught-proof doors and windows.

body.text: Energy cashback offers can stack with a cheaper tariff. Check the live offers in the app.

articles.title: Broadband & mobile
articles.summary: End-of-contract price rises, SIM-only and social tariffs.

body.text: Broadband and mobile are among the easiest bills to cut, mostly by not staying on out-of-contract prices.

items: Since 17 January 2025, price rises in new contracts must be shown in pounds and pence upfront
Providers must tell you when your contract is ending
Social tariffs are cheaper packages for people on certain benefits, such as Universal Credit

body.text: Save on broadband

items: Note your contract end date.
Check what speed you actually need.
Compare new-customer deals, then ask your provider to match or beat them.
Switch if they won't. Many switches are now provider-led and simple.

body.text: Save on mobile

items: Own your phone? SIM-only is usually far cheaper than a contract.
Compare total cost: a phone at £600 plus SIM-only at £12 a month for 24 months is £888, versus a £45-a-month contract at £1,080.
Check your actual data usage before choosing a plan.

articles.title: Council tax & water
articles.summary: Discounts, bands and water meters.

body.text: Council tax is based on your home's valuation band, but discounts and exemptions can cut it significantly.

items: Living alone (only adult): usually 25% off
Some people are “disregarded”, for example full-time students
Council Tax Reduction can help if you're on a low income

body.text: Check your band
If your band looks higher than similar homes nearby, you can check it with the Valuation Office Agency (in England and Wales). Bands can go down, but also up, so research first.
Water bills

items: A water meter often saves money if fewer people live in your home than there are bedrooms.
A sudden jump in usage could mean a leak. Contact your water company.
Ask about social tariffs if you're struggling to pay.

articles.title: Insurance renewals
articles.summary: When to shop around, renewal pricing rules and what cover you need.

body.text: Insurance is often one of the bills people overpay on, simply by auto-renewing without checking.

items: Since January 2022, home and car insurers can't charge renewing customers more than a new customer for the same policy
Quotes about 3–4 weeks before renewal are often cheaper than last-minute ones

body.text: Pay less without losing cover

items: Note your renewal date and start comparing about a month before.
Check the cover is right: excess, legal cover, courtesy car, contents limits.
Compare on more than one comparison site, and check direct-only insurers.
Pay annually if you can. Monthly payments often include interest.
Check for cashback on new policies.

body.text: Don't under-declare or leave out details to cut the price. It can invalidate your cover when you need it.

articles.title: Workplace pensions
articles.summary: Auto-enrolment, contributions and why opting out costs you.

body.text: A workplace pension is one of the best deals in personal finance: your employer adds money, and the government adds tax relief.

items: Employers must enrol eligible workers aged 22+ earning over £10,000 a year
Minimum total contribution: 8% of qualifying earnings, at least 3% from the employer
Opting out means losing your employer's contributions

body.text: Make the most of it

items: Check whether your employer matches extra contributions. Not taking a full match is leaving free money behind.
Salary sacrifice can save tax and National Insurance (check how it affects things like mortgage applications).
Check the default fund and its fees in your pension app.

body.text: Old pensions
Combining old pensions can make them easier to track and may cut fees. But check for exit fees or valuable guarantees before moving anything.
“Free pension review” cold calls are illegal in the UK, and a classic scam opener. Hang up.

articles.title: Pension tax relief & access
articles.summary: Tax relief, access age and the tax-free lump sum.

body.text: Pensions get tax relief on the way in, which makes them powerful for long-term saving. In exchange, you can't normally touch the money until later in life.

items: Annual allowance: £60,000 of tax-relieved contributions a year (lower for some high earners and people who've started drawing a pension)
Normal minimum pension age: 55, rising to 57 from 6 April 2028
Usually up to 25% can be taken tax-free, capped by the lump sum allowance (£268,275)

body.text: How tax relief works
Contributions get relief at your income tax rate. Basic-rate relief is often added automatically, and higher-rate taxpayers may need to claim the extra through Self Assessment.
Compounding over decades
£100 a month growing at 5% for 30 years becomes about £83,000, from £36,000 paid in.
Offers to unlock your pension before the minimum age usually mean huge tax charges, or that the money is stolen.
Pension Wise (part of MoneyHelper) offers free guidance from age 50.

articles.title: The State Pension
articles.summary: State Pension age, NI years and tracing lost pensions.

body.text: The State Pension is based on your National Insurance record, not on your earnings.

items: State Pension age is 66, rising to 67 between 2026 and 2028
You usually need 10 qualifying NI years to get any new State Pension, and 35 for the full amount
Check your forecast for free on gov.uk

body.text: Fill the gaps

items: Check your NI record for missing years.
Some gaps are filled by credits (e.g. claiming certain benefits or Child Benefit for a young child).
You may be able to pay voluntary contributions to fill gaps. Check whether it's worth it for you first.

body.text: Lost pensions
Use the government's free Pension Tracing Service to find old workplace or personal pensions.

articles.title: Stack £500 in 90 days
articles.summary: The step-by-step starter plan.

body.text: A simple 90-day plan to build habits and earn your first few hundred pounds from offers, without risking your main finances.
Days 1–7: foundations

items: Set up a spare current account to use only for switching.
Build a small cash buffer (£100–£500) so deposit requirements don't squeeze you.
Do the 20-minute subscription clear-out.
Sign up to one or two cashback sites.

body.text: Days 8–30: first switch

items: Pick one live switch offer you're eligible for. Read the full terms.
Write down every condition and deadline.
Start the CASS switch and set up Direct Debits early.
Add the payout to your tracker in the Money Hunters app.

body.text: Days 31–60: everyday savings

items: Start supermarket stacking on your weekly shop.
Route planned online purchases through cashback.
Review energy, broadband and mobile deals.

body.text: Days 61–90: grow

items: Once the first bonus lands, consider a second switch, spaced out.
Put bonuses towards your emergency fund or debt.
Review what worked and repeat it.

body.text: Never borrow to meet deposit requirements, and never sign up for products you don't understand. Bonuses are a nice extra, not a reason to take risks.

articles.title: Common mistakes
articles.summary: The errors that cost hunters their bonuses.

body.text: The most common ways hunters lose bonuses or money, and how to avoid them.

items: Not reading the full terms: missing one condition means no bonus.
Direct Debits not “active” by the deadline.
Paying in from the wrong source (e.g. an internal transfer when the offer needs an external one).
Closing an account too early and triggering a clawback.
Counting cashback before it's paid.
Using voucher codes that void cashback.
Stacking credit applications before a mortgage.
Letting free trials roll into paid subscriptions.
Buying things just because there's a bonus.
Trusting “offers” from strangers' links, or messages that pressure you.

body.text: The fix

items: Keep one tracker with every offer, its conditions and deadlines.
Set calendar reminders a week before each deadline.
Confirm details on the provider's own site.
When in doubt, skip it. There's always another offer.
